days.title: Edimburgo
days.sub: Día completo a pie por Old Town y New Town

tips.t: Lo que necesita luz va antes de las 15:45: castillo, Victoria Street y Calton Hill. El tour, los jardines y el mercado, ya de noche.
El tour de fantasmas es a hora fija (16:30–18:30). Todo lo demás se ordena alrededor.
Dean Village se quita solo por falta de luz. Si lo quieres, inclúyelo y quita los jardines.
La luz se va pronto: Calton Hill se coloca solo antes de la puesta de sol.
Con tanta luz puedes subir a Arthur's Seat después de cenar y ver allí el atardecer.
Si llueve, alarga el museo (es gratis) y acorta los paseos.

items.lead: Café pequeño de producto escocés, a 2 min de la Royal Mile. Full Scottish con haggis y black pudding.
eat: Full Scottish breakfast: huevos, bacon, salchicha, black pudding, tattie scone y a veces haggis.
Si quieres algo ligero: porridge con miel.
tips: Abre a las 7:30 entre semana. Es pequeño y se llena: mejor reservar.
Del Larder al castillo hay unos 15 min andando, cuesta arriba.
Lleva calzado cómodo: Old Town es adoquín y cuestas.
items.q: The Edinburgh Larder, 15 Blackfriars Street, Edinburgh

items.lead: La fortaleza sobre el volcán apagado. Lo primero del día, antes de las colas.
see: Honours of Scotland: la corona y la Piedra del Destino.
St Margaret's Chapel: el edificio más antiguo de la ciudad (s. XII).
Mons Meg, el cañón medieval gigante.
Vistas desde la Half Moon Battery.
tips: Entra a las 09:30 y ve directo a las joyas de la corona: luego hay cola.
One O'Clock Gun: cañonazo a las 13:00 (no los domingos). Si quieres verlo, entra a las 11:00.
La audioguía merece la pena si te gusta la historia.
30 de noviembre: San Andrés, festivo en Escocia. Casi todo abre igual; algunos años Historic Scotland regala o rebaja entradas ese fin de semana. Mira la web del castillo en noviembre.
items.book: Entrada con hora online (≈ £20). Con Explorer Pass también hay que reservar hora.
items.photo: Al castillo: desde la fuente Ross, en West Princes Street Gardens, con la fuente delante y la roca encima. Desde dentro: la explanada, hacia New Town.

items.lead: La calle principal de Old Town, del castillo hacia abajo. A mediodía St Giles' está abierta.
see: Catedral de St Giles' y su Thistle Chapel.
Heart of Midlothian: un corazón en el suelo. La tradición es escupir encima.
Los «closes»: callejones como Advocate's Close o Fleshmarket Close.
tips: Esta noche volverás a estos callejones con el tour de fantasmas: ahora míralos con luz.
items.photo: Advocate's Close, con el Scott Monument iluminado al fondo.
items.film: Vengadores: Infinity War (2018): St Giles’ y la Royal Mile salen en las escenas de Edimburgo.

items.lead: La parte más fotogénica de Old Town, cuesta abajo desde el castillo.
see: Victoria Street: la calle curva de colores que inspiró el Callejón Diagon.
Grassmarket: plaza de pubs donde antes estaba la horca (de ahí el pub The Last Drop).
Greyfriars Kirkyard: la tumba de «Thomas Riddell» y vistas a George Heriot's School.
Estatua de Greyfriars Bobby, el perro fiel.
tips: No frotes la nariz de Bobby: está estropeando la estatua.
El cementerio, mejor con luz.
items.photo: Desde Victoria Terrace, la pasarela de arriba: la curva entera con las fachadas de colores.
items.film: Harry Potter: Victoria Street es una de las calles que se dice inspiraron el callejón Diagon.

eat: Haggis, neeps & tatties: el plato nacional.
Cullen skink: sopa de eglefino ahumado, ideal con frío.
items.lead: Cocina escocesa de temporada en un edificio antiguo de Victoria Street: haggis, neeps & tatties y Cullen skink.
tips: Abre a mediodía todos los días. Con 45 min, pide sopa y un plato.

alts.ti: Comida en The White Hart Inn
alts.q: The White Hart Inn, 34 Grassmarket, Edinburgh
alts.lead: Pub de los más antiguos del Grassmarket. Haggis con neeps & tatties y una pinta.
tips: Abre a las 11:00 todos los días.

alts.lead: Cerdo asado en bocadillo con haggis y salsa de manzana. Rápido y barato; para comer de pie.
tips: De 11:00 a 17:00 o hasta que se acaba el cerdo.

items.lead: Antiguo pueblo de molinos a 15 min del centro. Parece de cuento.
see: Bell's Brae Bridge y las casas de Well Court.
El paseo del Water of Leith hasta Stockbridge.
Circus Lane: callejón de casitas con flores.
tips: Si vas cansado, ve en taxi o bus y vuelve andando.
Sin luz no merece la pena.

Piezas del ajedrez de Lewis.
El Grand Gallery, la sala principal de hierro y cristal.

Greyfriars Kirkyard de noche, si tu tour lo incluye.

routes.lead: Basada en tus enlaces: Scott Monument y Princes Street, subida por Cockburn Street a la Royal Mile y St Giles’, castillo a media mañana, bajada por Victoria Street y Greyfriars (Bobby y la tumba de Thomas Riddell), y Calton Hill a la puesta de sol antes del tour de las 16:30. De paso: Tron Kirk Market y la tienda Museum Context (las tienes como ideas para añadir). Sin museo.
routes.lead_en: Based on your links: Scott Monument and Princes Street, up Cockburn Street to the Royal Mile and St Giles’, castle mid-morning, down Victoria Street and Greyfriars (Bobby and Thomas Riddell’s grave), and Calton Hill at sunset before the 16:30 tour. On the way: Tron Kirk Market and the Museum Context shop (as ideas to add). No museum.

routes.lead: Sin bucles y con las dos horas fijas (Calton Hill al atardecer y el tour de las 16:30). Por la mañana: The Balmoral, Scott Monument, Waverley Bridge, subida por Warriston’s Close a la Royal Mile (tiendas) y New College; castillo en 2 h; bajada a The Vennel, Victoria Street y Greyfriars (Harry Potter) con la tienda Museum Context y comida rápida en Oink. Por la noche, el reloj iluminado del Canongate Tolbooth antes del mercado de Navidad. Fuera: museo, St Cuthbert’s y Circus Lane.
routes.lead_en: Loop-free and with both fixed times (Calton Hill at sunset and the 16:30 tour). Morning: The Balmoral, Scott Monument, Waverley Bridge, up Warriston’s Close to the Royal Mile (shops) and New College; castle in 2 h; down to The Vennel, Victoria Street and Greyfriars (Harry Potter) with the Museum Context shop and a quick lunch at Oink. At night, the lit Canongate Tolbooth clock before the Christmas market. Left out: museum, St Cuthbert’s and Circus Lane.

driving.t: Conduces por la izquierda y adelantas por la derecha. Los primeros días, piensa «izquierda» en cada cruce y al salir de gasolineras y parkings.
Se giran en sentido horario. Cede el paso a quien viene por tu derecha, ya dentro de la rotonda.
70 mph (113 km/h) en autovía, 60 mph (97) en carretera, 30 mph (48) en pueblos. En buena parte de Edimburgo, 20 mph (32).
Cajas fijas, furgonetas móviles y radares de tramo en la A9 entre Dunblane e Inverness: miden tu velocidad media.
Si viene alguien, para en el «passing place» a tu izquierda o espera frente al de la derecha. Deja pasar a quien venga detrás. Saluda: es costumbre.
Mira la etiqueta: «Unleaded» es gasolina y «Diesel», diésel. En la A87 y la A82 hay pocas gasolineras: no bajes de medio depósito.
Límite 0,5 g/l en sangre (0,22 mg/l en aire), más estricto que en Inglaterra. Lo seguro es no beber nada.
Prohibido usarlo en la mano, incluso parado en un semáforo. Solo en soporte y con manos libres.
Doble línea amarilla: prohibido siempre. Línea simple: mira el horario del cartel. Muchos parkings se pagan en máquina o con app.
Edimburgo y Glasgow tienen zona de bajas emisiones y carriles bus con horario y cámaras. Mejor aparcar y moverse a pie.
Mira Traffic Scotland y los avisos del Met Office. Con aviso de nieve o hielo, sal más tarde y con luz.
Al amanecer, al anochecer, en sombra, puentes y curvas de montaña. Si el asfalto parece mojado y hace 0–3 °C, trátalo como hielo.
Marchas largas, acelerador suave y hasta 10 veces más distancia con el de delante. Frena antes y con suavidad.
No frenes de golpe. Suelta el acelerador y gira suave hacia donde quieres ir.
Arranca en segunda. En subidas mantén un ritmo constante sin pararte. Quita la nieve del techo y de las luces antes de salir.
Con lluvia, niebla o nieve, cortas encendidas también de día. Antiniebla traseras solo con menos de 100 m de visibilidad.
Rascador, manta, agua, algo de comer, linterna, cargador y depósito por encima de la mitad.
Sobre todo al amanecer y al anochecer en la A9, A82 y A87. Si ves uno, frena: suelen ir en grupo. Sin volantazos.
Paso de Drumochter (A9, 462 m), Glen Shiel y Cluanie (A87) y Rannoch Moor (A82): los primeros con nieve y viento.
En Rannoch Moor y Glencoe las rachas mueven el coche. Las dos manos al volante y cuidado al adelantar camiones.
Policía, ambulancia, bomberos y rescate de montaña. Funciona aunque no tengas saldo.
Llama a la asistencia del alquiler (número en el contrato o en el parabrisas). Sal del coche por el lado contrario al tráfico si es seguro.
Para siempre, intercambia datos y haz fotos. Si hay heridos, 999. Avisa a la empresa de alquiler.
Hay tramos sin señal. Lleva mapas offline y la dirección del hotel guardada. La app what3words la usan los servicios de emergencia británicos para localizarte.

groups.ti_en: On the way along the A82 (day 4)

d1.title: Edinburgh
d1.sub: A full day on foot through the Old Town and New Town
tips: What needs daylight goes before 15:45: the castle, Victoria Street and Calton Hill. The tour, the gardens and the market come after dark.
The ghost tour has a fixed time (16:30–18:30). Everything else is arranged around it.
Dean Village is dropped automatically for lack of light. If you want it, add it back and remove the gardens.
Light goes early: Calton Hill is placed automatically before sunset.
With so much light you can climb Arthur’s Seat after dinner and watch the sunset there.
If it rains, spend longer in the museum (it’s free) and shorten the walks.

d2.title: On to Inverness
d2.sub: Stirling, Dunkeld and Queen’s View along the A9
tips: Short day: you leave at 07:30 and The Kelpies is dropped automatically. That way you reach Queen’s View before sunset.
Pitlochry and the drive to Inverness will be after dark. Check the forecast for the Drumochter Pass: it can snow.
Plenty of light: you can add Blair Castle or the Pass of Killiecrankie, 15 minutes from Pitlochry.
Explorer Pass: Edinburgh + Stirling + Urquhart already cost more than the pass.

d3.title: Loch Ness and Eilean Donan
d3.sub: From Loch Ness to the west coast and down to Fort William
tips: Short day: Invermoriston and the Commando Memorial are dropped automatically. You reach Eilean Donan in daylight and watch the sunset there.
The drive down to Fort William will be in the dark: the A87 has bends and deer. Take it easy.
Glen Shiel in low light is beautiful: make the stops on the way out, not on the way back.
Eilean Donan: check on its website that it is open that day. If it is closed, the outside alone is worth the trip.
Fuel: fill up in Inverness or Fort Augustus. There are few petrol stations on the A87.

d4.title: Highlands, Glasgow and home
d4.sub: Glenfinnan, Glencoe, Loch Lomond, Glasgow and Edinburgh Airport
tips: Short day: Glenfinnan, Glencoe and Rannoch Moor in daylight; Glen Etive is dropped automatically. Glasgow after dark with the Christmas lights.

You return the car around 20:30 and the flight is in the early hours: you have time to spare. Stay longer in Glasgow or stop at South Queensferry to see the Forth Bridge lit up, 15 minutes from the airport.
Prioritise Glencoe and Rannoch Moor in daylight. Luss is the first thing you can drop.
With plenty of light, do the whole of Glen Etive and stop at Loch Tulla.
It’s the longest day: don’t leave anything at the hotel or in the car when you return it.

d1-des.lead: Small café with Scottish produce, 2 min from the Royal Mile. Full Scottish with haggis and black pudding.
eat: Full Scottish breakfast: eggs, bacon, sausage, black pudding, tattie scone and sometimes haggis.
Something lighter: porridge with honey.
tips: Opens 7:30 on weekdays. It’s small and fills up: book ahead.
From the Larder to the castle is about 15 min on foot, uphill.
Wear comfortable shoes: the Old Town is cobbles and hills.

d1-castillo.lead: The fortress on the extinct volcano. First thing in the day, before the queues.
see: Honours of Scotland: the crown and the Stone of Destiny.
St Margaret’s Chapel: the oldest building in the city (12th century).
Mons Meg, the giant medieval cannon.
Views from the Half Moon Battery.
tips: Go in at 09:30 and head straight to the Crown Jewels: the queue builds later.
One O’Clock Gun: fired at 13:00 (not on Sundays). To see it, go in at 11:00.
The audio guide is worth it if you like history.
30 November: St Andrew’s Day, a holiday in Scotland. Almost everything opens as usual; some years Historic Scotland gives away or discounts tickets that weekend. Check the castle website in November.
d1-castillo.book: Timed ticket online (≈ £20). With the Explorer Pass you still need to book a time.
d1-castillo.photo: The castle: from the Ross Fountain in West Princes Street Gardens, fountain in front and the rock above. From inside: the esplanade, towards New Town.

d1-royal.lead: The Old Town’s main street, from the castle downhill. At midday St Giles’ is open.
see: St Giles’ Cathedral and its Thistle Chapel.
Heart of Midlothian: a heart in the pavement. Tradition says you spit on it.
The closes: alleys such as Advocate’s Close or Fleshmarket Close.
tips: Tonight you’ll be back in these alleys on the ghost tour: see them in daylight now.
d1-royal.photo: Advocate’s Close, with the Scott Monument lit up behind.
d1-royal.film: Avengers: Infinity War (2018): St Giles’ and the Royal Mile appear in the Edinburgh scenes.

d1-victoria.lead: The most photogenic part of the Old Town, downhill from the castle.
see: Victoria Street: the curved, colourful street that inspired Diagon Alley.
Grassmarket: a square of pubs where the gallows once stood (hence the pub The Last Drop).
Greyfriars Kirkyard: the grave of “Thomas Riddell” and views of George Heriot’s School.
The statue of Greyfriars Bobby, the loyal dog.
tips: Don’t rub Bobby’s nose: it is wearing the statue away.
The kirkyard is better in daylight.
d1-victoria.photo: From Victoria Terrace, the upper walkway: the whole curve with its coloured shopfronts.
d1-victoria.film: Harry Potter: Victoria Street is one of the streets said to have inspired Diagon Alley.

eat: Haggis, neeps & tatties: the national dish.
Cullen skink: smoked haddock soup, perfect in the cold.
d1-comida.lead: Seasonal Scottish food in an old Victoria Street building: haggis, neeps & tatties and Cullen skink.
tips: Open from midday every day. With 45 min, have soup and one dish.

d1-dean.lead: An old mill village 15 minutes from the centre. It looks like a fairy tale.
see: Bell’s Brae Bridge and the Well Court houses.
The Water of Leith walkway to Stockbridge.
Circus Lane: a lane of cottages with flowers.
tips: If you are tired, take a taxi or bus and walk back.
Without daylight it isn’t worth it.
d1-dean.photo: From the Bells Brae bridge over the river: the Well Court houses with the water in front.

d1-museo.lead: Free and indoors, next to Greyfriars. A short visit before going up Calton Hill.
see: Dolly the cloned sheep.
Pieces of the Lewis Chessmen.
The Grand Gallery, the main iron-and-glass hall.
tips: Go straight to what interests you: Dolly and the Lewis Chessmen.

d1-calton.lead: The city’s best balcony. It is scheduled automatically 40 minutes before sunset.
see: Dugald Stewart Monument: the classic photo with the castle and the Balmoral clock tower.
National Monument: the “Parthenon” that was never finished.
Nelson Monument.
tips: The best light is before sunset, not after.
It is very windy at the top: gloves and hat.
Head down once the city lights come on: worth the wait.
d1-calton.photo: By the Dugald Stewart Monument, looking west: the Old Town, the castle and Princes Street.

d1-fantasmas.lead: Two hours through the alleys, graveyards and underground vaults of the Old Town, after dark.
see: South Bridge Vaults: chambers under the bridge, the most visited on these tours.
Royal Mile closes: stories of plague, crime and body snatchers.
Greyfriars Kirkyard at night, if your tour includes it.
tips: Arrive 10 minutes early at the meeting point.
It is cold and damp underground: coat and closed shoes.
From Calton Hill it is about a 15-minute walk to the Royal Mile.

d1-gardens.ti: Princes Street Gardens and the Scott Monument
d1-gardens.lead: Gardens below the castle, lit up at night. Right next to the market.
see: The castle from below: the most famous view.
Scott Monument: 287 steps and 360° views.
tips: The Scott Monument closes early in winter: at night, admire it from below.
d1-gardens.photo: The Scott Monument from East Princes Street Gardens; in December, with the market lights.

d1-navidad.lead: Edinburgh’s Christmas: stalls, mulled wine and a big wheel next to the Scott Monument.
see: The big wheel, with the lit-up castle behind.
Food stalls: try mulled wine or a hot toddy.
tips: It usually runs from mid-November to early January. Check the dates.
Some rides need a timed ticket.

eat: Haggis bon bons to start.
Venison or Scottish salmon as a main.
tips: Kitchen until 21:30. It’s small: book.
d1-cena.lead: Pub-restaurant in a close off the Royal Mile. Scottish food and a huge whisky list.

see: Sandy Bell’s: live music almost every night.
The Bow Bar (Victoria St): hundreds of whiskies.
tips: Only if you have energy left: tomorrow you leave at 07:30.
It’s St Andrew’s Day: it may be busy, go early.

d2-coche.lead: Take your time here: it avoids surprises when you return it.
tips: Check when the office opens: in winter it pays to leave early.
Take photos and video of the car outside, inside and of the fuel gauge.
Ask whether it is petrol or diesel. In the UK the green nozzle is petrol and the black one diesel.
Ask for an ice scraper and check the lights work.
Drive on the left. At roundabouts give way to the right and go clockwise.

d2-kelpies.lead: Two 30-metre steel horse heads. A quick, free stop.
tips: The car park is paid.
If you are short of time, this is the first thing to drop.
d2-kelpies.photo: From the canal path, head-on, both heads together; they are lit up at dusk.

d2-stirling.lead: For many, prettier than Edinburgh’s and less crowded.
see: The restored Great Hall.
The Royal Palace and the “Stirling Heads”, carved wooden medallions.
Views of the Wallace Monument and the bridge of the 1297 battle.
tips: Opens at 09:30.
The Wallace Monument is 246 steps. In winter there is no time: you can see it from the castle.
d2-stirling.book: ≈ £19 online. Included in the Explorer Pass.
d2-stirling.photo: The castle: from the King’s Knot, the geometric garden below. From the walls: the Wallace Monument.

tips: M9 and A9 via Perth.

d2-dunkeld.lead: A small village by the River Tay and a forest of giant firs.
see: Dunkeld Cathedral: half in ruins, on the banks of the Tay. Free.
Telford’s bridge (1809).
The Hermitage: the Black Linn waterfall and Ossian’s Hall.
eat: Aran Bakery: the village’s famous bakery. It closes early.
tips: The Hermitage: paid parking (NTS) and a flat 1 km walk. It may be muddy or icy.
d2-dunkeld.photo: From Ossian’s Hall, the balcony over the Black Linn falls.

tips: On the A9 to Pitlochry, then the B8019.

d2-queens.lead: Viewpoint over Loch Tummel with Schiehallion behind.
tips: With the low afternoon light it is the best stop of the day.
There is a café by the viewpoint, with short winter hours.
d2-queens.photo: From the viewpoint railing, looking west: Loch Tummel on the diagonal and Schiehallion behind.

d2-pitlochry.lead: A Victorian town of whisky, wool and mountains. Nice at night too.
see: The main street, with wool and whisky shops.
The dam and its salmon ladder, 5 minutes on foot.
tips: Blair Athol and Edradour distilleries: winter hours are shorter. Check the website or book.
A good place for a hot tea before the long stretch.
The A9 has average speed cameras.
You cross the Cairngorms and the Drumochter Pass. At night, watch out for deer.

eat: Hootananny: pub with live traditional music.
The Mustard Seed: Scottish food in an old church.
tips: In winter food is served until 22:00.
d2-cena.lead: Ale tavern next to Inverness Castle, with a dining room upstairs. Haggis, Cullen skink and local salmon.

tips: Take the A82, along the west shore of the loch.

d3-urquhart.lead: The most famous ruins on Loch Ness, on a point above the water.
see: The Grant Tower: climb it for the best view of the loch.
A replica trebuchet.
The short film at the entrance: at the end the curtain opens onto the castle.
tips: Arrive at opening time: the coaches come later.
Fact: the loch is 37 km long and holds more water than all the lakes in England and Wales combined.
d3-urquhart.book: Book online (≈ £15). Included in the Explorer Pass.
d3-urquhart.photo: From the path down from the visitor centre: Grant Tower with the loch behind.

d3-inver.lead: Telford’s old bridge and a waterfall 2 minutes from the car park.
d3-inver.photo: From Telford’s old bridge over the river; the falls are 5 min along the path.

d3-fa.lead: A village at the southern tip of the loch, split in two by the Caledonian Canal.
see: The flight of 5 locks.
The pier, with a view down the whole of Loch Ness.
eat: Early lunch in a pub by the locks, such as The Lock Inn.
If it’s too early to eat, buy something and have it at the Eilean Donan café.

d3-r4.lead: The prettiest drive of the day: the A82 to Invergarry, then the A87.
tips: Stop at the Glengarry viewpoint: the loch is shaped like a map of Scotland.
Glen Shiel and the Five Sisters of Kintail: find a lay-by and stop.
In winter there may be ice on the A87 passes.

d3-eilean.lead: The postcard castle: an islet where three lochs meet, with a stone bridge.
see: Rebuilt between 1912 and 1932 on 13th-century ruins.
It appears in “Highlander” and “The World Is Not Enough”.
tips: No photos inside.
Hours change by season and it closes for a few weeks in winter. Check the website before you go.
d3-eilean.photo: From the shore by the car park, with the bridge on the diagonal. For the view from above, drive up to Carr Brae above Dornie.
d3-eilean.film: Highlander (1986) and “The World Is Not Enough” (James Bond, 1999) were filmed here.

d3-eileansun.lead: In winter the sun sets mid-afternoon: stay for the last light over the three lochs.
tips: While you wait, a hot tea in the visitor centre café.
At dusk they usually switch on the castle lights.
d3-eileansun.photo: From the shore by the car park: castle and bridge against the light.
d3-eileansun.film: The castle from “Highlander” and “The World Is Not Enough”.

tips: Back along the A87 to Invergarry and down the A82.

d3-commando.lead: Memorial to the WWII commandos with Ben Nevis behind.
d3-commando.photo: The three figures from behind, looking at the mountains.

eat: Crannog: fish and seafood on the pier.
Grog & Gruel: pub with local beers.
Ben Nevis Inn: at the foot of the mountain, with a hikers’ atmosphere.
tips: Winter hours change: check or book ahead.
d3-cena.lead: The Crannog seafood restaurant left the pier and now cooks inside the Garrison West pub: fish and shellfish from the loch.

tips: Pack the boot neatly: you won’t be back at the hotel today.
Prepare a small bag with what you need for the flight.

d4-glenfinnan.lead: The Hogwarts Express viaduct and the loch where the 1745 Jacobite rising began.
see: The 21-arch viaduct (1901).
The 1815 Jacobite monument by Loch Shiel.
tips: Walk up to the viewpoint on the path behind the visitor centre (15–20 min). It can be slippery.
The car park is paid.
The steam train only runs from April to October.
d4-glenfinnan.photo: From the high viewpoint (15 min path from the visitor centre): the curving viaduct with the loch behind.
d4-glenfinnan.film: Harry Potter: the Hogwarts Express crosses this viaduct in four films; in “Chamber of Secrets” the flying car chases it through the arches. Loch Shiel, next to it, is the Black Lake.

d4-tren.lead: The steam train crosses the viaduct towards Mallaig at around 10:45.
tips: This is an approximate time: check it on the day.
Be at the viewpoint 20–30 minutes early: it fills up.
d4-tren.photo: From the viaduct’s high viewpoint; be there 15 min before the train.
d4-tren.film: Harry Potter: this steam train is the Hogwarts Express (runs April to October).

tips: Back through Fort William and south on the A82.

d4-sisters.lead: Three mountains in a row above the glen. The classic image of Glencoe.
tips: There are several lay-bys on the A82; the big one is the most famous.
Be careful crossing the road.
d4-sisters.photo: From the A82 viewpoint car park, looking south: the three ridges in a row.

d4-buachaille.lead: The pyramid mountain with the white Lagangarbh cottage in front.
d4-buachaille.photo: From the Altnafeadh car park, with the white Lagangarbh hut and the river in front.
d4-buachaille.film: Skyfall (2012): James Bond stops the Aston Martin on the A82 with this mountain behind.

eat: Kingshouse Hotel, 5 min from the Buachaille: deer often wander by the car park.
Clachaig Inn: legendary mountain pub, 15 min back.
see: If you head back west, the Glencoe Visitor Centre tells the story of the 1692 massacre.
d4-comida.lead: Historic inn below Buachaille Etive Mòr. The Way Inn bar and restaurant: game, seafood and traditional dishes.
tips: Lunch 12:00–16:15. Book a table: they ask even just for drinks.
Deer often wander by the car park.

d4-etive.lead: A single-track road through a wild glen. It appears in “Skyfall”.
tips: Only if you have time and daylight.
d4-etive.film: Skyfall: Glen Etive is the glen on the way to the Bond family home.

d4-r3.lead: The most “Highland” stretch of the trip: moorland, lochs and mountains.
tips: Stop at the Loch Tulla viewpoint, past Rannoch Moor.
Tyndrum: The Green Welly Stop or the Real Food Café for a coffee.
d4-r3.film: Harry Potter: on Rannoch Moor the Hogwarts Express is stopped in “Deathly Hallows Part 1”.

d4-luss.lead: A village of stone cottages and a pier on the largest loch in Great Britain.
d4-luss.photo: From Luss pier, looking up the loch towards Ben Lomond.

tips: Central Glasgow is a Low Emission Zone (LEZ). Modern rental cars usually comply: check when you pick it up.
Park in a city-centre car park and walk.

d4-glasgow.lead: Less postcard than Edinburgh, more of a real city: murals, Victorian architecture and atmosphere.
see: The Duke of Wellington with a traffic cone on his head (GoMA).
Buchanan Street and George Square with the City Chambers.
In December, lights and a Christmas market in the centre (usually in George Square or St Enoch Square).
The city-centre murals: St Mungo, on High Street, is the most famous.
tips: The cathedral and the Necropolis keep daytime hours: at night, see them from outside.

eat: Sloans (Argyll Arcade): bar-restaurant dating from 1797.
Mother India: curry. Glasgow claims it invented tikka masala.
Ubiquitous Chip (Ashton Lane): Scottish food in a covered courtyard.
d4-cena.lead: Bar-restaurant from 1797 inside the Argyll Arcade, one of Glasgow’s oldest: Scottish dishes and fish & chips.
tips: Open every day from 11:30.
On the M8. No tolls.
Full-to-full policy: refuel as close to the airport as possible.
Keep the receipt.
If the desk is closed there is usually a key drop box. Ask when you pick the car up.
Photos and video of the car, the mileage and the full tank.
Check the glovebox and boot: sunglasses, chargers, documents.
Check whether the terminal and security are open overnight. They usually open in the early hours.
Charged power bank and a warm layer: the terminal is cold at night.
Boarding pass in Wallet.

x-nms.lead: Free. Dolly the sheep, cars, dinosaurs and a roof terrace with castle views.

x-greyfriars.lead: A 17th-century graveyard and the statue of Bobby the dog, 2 minutes from Victoria Street.
x-greyfriars.film: Harry Potter: here is Thomas Riddell’s gravestone, often linked to Tom Riddle; from the kirkyard you can see George Heriot’s School, said to have inspired Hogwarts.

x-dean.lead: An old mill village by the river, a 15-minute walk from Princes Street.
x-dean.photo: From the Bells Brae bridge over the river: the Well Court houses with the water in front.

x-circus.lead: A curved lane of small houses with flowers, and neighbourhood cafés.
x-circus.photo: From the west end of Circus Lane, at the bend: colourful mews houses with St Stephen’s tower behind.

x-gallery.lead: Free. Scottish and European painting between the Old and New Towns.

x-holyrood.lead: The King’s residence in Scotland and the abbey ruins. Fewer opening days in winter: check the hours.

x-holyrude.lead: A 15th-century church next to the castle, where James VI was crowned.

x-hermitage.lead: A forest of giant firs and the Black Linn waterfall, 5 minutes from Dunkeld.
x-hermitage.photo: From Ossian’s Hall, the balcony over the Black Linn falls.

x-queensview.lead: A viewpoint over Loch Tummel, 10 minutes from Pitlochry.
x-queensview.photo: From the viewpoint railing, looking west: Loch Tummel on the diagonal and Schiehallion behind.

x-culloden.lead: Visitor centre for the 1746 battle and the moor where it was fought. 15 minutes from Inverness.

x-plockton.lead: A fishing village with palm trees by the loch, 25 minutes from Eilean Donan.
x-plockton.photo: From Harbour Street by the water: boats, palm trees and cottages.

x-skyebridge.lead: Cross briefly to the Isle of Skye and back: 15 minutes from Eilean Donan.
x-skyebridge.photo: From Kyleakin harbour, on Skye, looking at the bridge.

x-commando.lead: A memorial with views of Ben Nevis, 15 minutes from Fort William.

x-neptune.lead: Eight locks in a row on the Caledonian Canal with Ben Nevis behind.

x-glennevis.lead: The glen at the foot of Ben Nevis, 5 minutes from Fort William. Lovely early in the morning.
x-glennevis.photo: From the bridge at the Lower Falls (Polldubh), water tumbling between rocks.
x-glennevis.film: Harry Potter: Steall Falls in Glen Nevis is where Harry faces the Hungarian Horntail (“Goblet of Fire”); about 45–60 min on foot from the car park at the end of the glen.

x-falloch.lead: A waterfall 2 minutes from the car park, right by the A82.
x-falloch.photo: From the metal viewing platform over the falls.

x-kelvingrove.lead: Free. Dalí’s Christ, an organ and a spectacular building.

x-riverside.lead: Free. Trams, cars and an old Glasgow street, with an 1896 tall ship outside.

x-kelpies.lead: Two 30 m steel horse heads, lit up at night. On the way to the airport.
x-kelpies.photo: From the canal path, head-on, both heads together; they are lit up at dusk.

a-camera.lead: Five floors of optical illusions and a 19th-century camera obscura projecting the city live.
tips: A good plan if it rains.
It closes later than the museums: check the hours.

a-whiskyexp.lead: A tour with tasting next to the castle and a huge collection of bottles.
tips: Book the tour with tasting.

a-marykings.lead: Guided tour of 17th-century streets buried under the Royal Mile.
tips: Book: places go fast.
Not for you if enclosed spaces bother you.

a-panda.lead: A speakeasy hidden behind a fake barber’s shop. Signature cocktails.
tips: You go in through the “barber’s” and down a staircase.

a-bowbar.ti: Whisky tasting at The Bow Bar
a-bowbar.lead: A small pub with hundreds of whiskies. Order a few to compare.
tips: Try one from Speyside and one from Islay to taste the difference.

a-rest.ti: A quiet night at the hotel
a-rest.lead: Tomorrow you leave at 07:30: resting is a plan too.

a-blairathol.lead: The town’s distillery, the heart of Bell’s whisky. Guided tour with tasting.
tips: Fewer tours in winter: book.

a-westend.ti: West End: university and Ashton Lane
a-westend.lead: The Gothic cloisters of the University of Glasgow and the bar lane of Ashton Lane.
tips: The cloisters look like Hogwarts.
Park near Byres Road.

x-camera.lead: Optical illusions on five floors and views from the roof terrace.
x-camera.photo: From the rooftop terrace: Old Town roofs, Princes Street and the castle next door.

x-marykings.lead: 17th-century streets buried under the Royal Mile. Booking needed.

x-tartan.lead: Working looms and a huge tartan and wool shop next to the castle.

x-coffee.lead: A break with a scone and tea, looking up at the castle.

x-arthur.lead: The city’s volcano: 251 m and 360° views. About a 45-minute climb.
x-arthur.photo: From the summit: the whole city, the castle and the sea. On the way down, the city from Salisbury Crags.

x-panda.lead: A speakeasy hidden behind a fake barber’s shop.

x-wallace.lead: An 1869 tower with 246 steps and William Wallace’s sword.
x-wallace.photo: The monument: from Stirling Castle’s walls. From the top: the meandering River Forth.

x-blair.lead: Guided tour with tasting in the town centre.

x-dam.lead: A short walk along the dam and the ladder salmon use to swim upriver.

x-nessisl.lead: Suspension bridges over the River Ness, 15 minutes from the centre.

x-fuel2.lead: One of the cheapest in the north. Tomorrow there are no petrol stations between Fort Augustus and Kyle of Lochalsh: arrive with a full tank.

x-fuel3.lead: The last big petrol station before Glencoe and Tyndrum, where there are hardly any. Better today than tomorrow in a rush.

x-cruise.lead: Departs from Fort Augustus. Few sailings in winter: check the website.

x-centre.lead: An exhibition about the loch and the Nessie legend.

x-bnd.lead: Local whisky. Check the winter hours.

x-glencoevc.lead: The story of the glen and the 1692 massacre.

x-necro.lead: A medieval cathedral and a hill of Victorian tombs with views.
x-necro.photo: From the top of the Necropolis by the John Knox column: the cathedral and the city.

x-potstill.lead: Hundreds of whiskies in a small pub.

x-ashton.lead: A cobbled lane of bars and lights, next to the university.

x-queensferry.lead: The three bridges over the Firth of Forth, 15 minutes from the airport. The red one, from 1890, is a World Heritage Site.
x-queensferry.photo: From Hawes Pier in South Queensferry: the red bridge lit above the water.

a-whitehart.ti: Lunch at The White Hart Inn
a-whitehart.lead: One of the oldest pubs in the Grassmarket. Haggis with neeps & tatties and a pint.
tips: Opens 11:00 every day.

a-oink.lead: Hog roast roll with haggis and apple sauce. Quick and cheap; eat standing.
tips: 11:00–17:00 or until the pork runs out.

a-arcade.ti: Dinner at Arcade Haggis & Whisky House
a-arcade.lead: Small bar specialising in haggis and whisky. Very traditional.
tips: Kitchen closes at 21:00: 19:45 is tight, book.

a-no27.lead: Castle Street bar-restaurant: in the evening, traditional dishes with local produce (venison, beef).

a-crofter.lead: Classic High Street bar-restaurant, open all year: homemade soups and pub dishes.

a-maltman.ti: Dinner at The Malt Man (formerly Grog & Gruel)
a-maltman.lead: The old Grog & Gruel, under new owners since November 2025: whisky bar with pub food.
tips: The upstairs restaurant opens mainly in summer; in winter there may be bar food only.

a-clachaig.lead: Legendary mountain inn in Glen Coe; hearty pub food.
tips: In winter it opens 4 days a week: call ahead (01855 811252).

a-horseshoe.ti: Dinner at The Horse Shoe Bar
a-horseshoe.lead: Victorian gin palace from 1884 with a very long horseshoe-shaped bar. Cheap pub food.

a-chip.lead: A Scottish food classic since 1971, in a covered courtyard in the West End. Pricier: book.

x-ph-calton.lead: From the Dugald Stewart Monument: Princes Street, the Balmoral clock and the castle behind.
tips: In the rain headlights and wet tarmac shine: best at dusk (around 16:00 in December).
x-ph-calton.photo: From the Dugald Stewart Monument, looking west.

x-ph-tolbooth.lead: The 1591 tower with its clock hanging over the Royal Mile. Shoot from the opposite pavement, looking up the street.
tips: In @iangblack’s guide it is called “Old Tolbooth”.
x-ph-tolbooth.photo: From the opposite pavement, looking up the street, clock in the foreground.

x-ph-warriston.lead: A close with 100+ steps between the Royal Mile and Cockburn Street. From the top, wide angle, towards the rooftops.
tips: Wet steps are slippery: take care.
People live here: keep it quiet.
x-ph-warriston.photo: From the top of the steps, looking down.

x-ph-waverley.lead: The bridge over the station: Old Town skyline, the Scott Monument and trains below.
tips: A coloured umbrella in the foreground works great in the rain.
x-ph-waverley.photo: From the middle of the bridge, towards the Old Town and the Scott Monument.
x-ph-waverley.film: Avengers: Infinity War: the Scarlet Witch and Vision fight was shot at Waverley Station, by Calton Road; on Cockburn Street they watch the news.

x-ph-newcollege.lead: The university’s Gothic Revival courtyard at the top of the Mound, with the Assembly Hall towers.
tips: The courtyard is usually open during university hours.
x-ph-newcollege.photo: From the courtyard, towards the Assembly Hall towers.

x-ph-victoria.lead: The curving street of coloured shopfronts. From above, on Victoria Terrace.
tips: Busy by day: go early or after dark with the shops lit.
x-ph-victoria.photo: From Victoria Terrace, the upper walkway.
x-ph-victoria.film: Harry Potter: one of the streets said to have inspired Diagon Alley.

x-ph-vennel.lead: Steps by the Flodden Wall with the castle framed at the end. Edinburgh’s most famous photo.

x-ph-cuthbert.lead: St Cuthbert’s churchyard right below the castle: gravestones in front, the rock above.
tips: Enter from Lothian Road or from Princes Street Gardens.
x-ph-cuthbert.photo: From the churchyard, gravestones in front and the castle above.

x-ph-carlowrie.lead: Victorian castle about 15 km from the centre, near the airport. A private wedding and events venue.
tips: Not open to the public: only with the estate’s permission (carlowriecastle.co.uk).
You need a car.
x-ph-carlowrie.photo: Only with the estate’s permission: from the drive.

x-balmoral.film: Harry Potter: J. K. Rowling finished the last book here, in 2007.
x-balmoral.lead: The clock-tower hotel at the end of Princes Street, by the station.

x-hp-heriot.film: Harry Potter: this school, with its four houses, is said to have inspired Hogwarts. It is a working school: see it from the gates on Lauriston Place.
x-hp-heriot.lead: 17th-century building next to Greyfriars, with towers and a courtyard.
x-hp-heriot.photo: From the gates on Lauriston Place or the top of Greyfriars Kirkyard.

x-hp-torren.film: Harry Potter: Hagrid’s hut was built beside this lochan for “Prisoner of Azkaban”. It is gone, but the scenery is the same.

x-hp-torren.photo: From the shore, with the mountains behind.

driving.t: You drive on the left and overtake on the right. For the first few days, think “left” at every junction and when leaving petrol stations and car parks.
Go round clockwise. Give way to traffic coming from your right, already on the roundabout.
70 mph (113 km/h) on motorways and dual carriageways, 60 mph (97) on other roads, 30 mph (48) in villages. Much of Edinburgh is 20 mph (32).
Fixed yellow boxes, mobile vans and average speed cameras on the A9 between Dunblane and Inverness: they measure your average speed.
If someone is coming, pull into the passing place on your left or wait opposite one on the right. Let faster cars behind you pass. Wave: it’s the custom.
Check the label: “Unleaded” is petrol and “Diesel” is diesel. There are few petrol stations on the A87 and A82: don’t go below half a tank.
Limit 0.5 g/l in blood (0.22 mg/l in breath), stricter than in England. The safe choice is not to drink at all.
Using it in your hand is illegal, even when stopped at lights. Only in a holder and hands-free.
Double yellow line: never. Single line: check the times on the sign. Many car parks are paid at a machine or by app.
Edinburgh and Glasgow have low emission zones and bus lanes with times and cameras. Better to park and walk.
Check Traffic Scotland and the Met Office warnings. With a snow or ice warning, leave later and in daylight.
At dawn, at dusk, in shade, on bridges and mountain bends. If the road looks wet and it is 0–3 °C, treat it as ice.
Higher gears, gentle on the accelerator and up to 10 times more distance from the car ahead. Brake earlier and gently.
Don’t slam on the brakes. Ease off the accelerator and steer gently where you want to go.
Pull away in second gear. Keep a steady pace uphill without stopping. Clear snow from the roof and lights before setting off.
In rain, fog or snow, dipped headlights on, even by day. Rear fog lights only when visibility is under 100 m.
Scraper, blanket, water, something to eat, torch, charger and more than half a tank.
Mainly at dawn and dusk on the A9, A82 and A87. If you see one, slow down: they often come in groups. No sudden swerves.
Drumochter Pass (A9, 462 m), Glen Shiel and Cluanie (A87) and Rannoch Moor (A82): the first to get snow and wind.
On Rannoch Moor and in Glencoe gusts push the car. Both hands on the wheel and care when overtaking lorries.
Police, ambulance, fire and mountain rescue. Works even without credit.
Call the rental company’s assistance (number on the contract or the windscreen). Get out on the side away from traffic if it is safe.
Always stop, exchange details and take photos. If anyone is hurt, call 999. Tell the rental company.
Some stretches have no signal. Carry offline maps and keep the hotel address saved. British emergency services use the what3words app to locate you.
